concept.name: Optimistic Concurrency Control

relationships.description: Connects Optimistic Concurrency Control to database indexing in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A lock-free concurrency pattern that lets readers and writers proceed without blocking, validating at commit time via a version number or ETag that no one else modified the record.
spark.keyTakeaway: Use atomic compare-and-swap (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` or HTTP `If-Match`) when conflicts are rare (<5%), and pair retries with exponential backoff and full jitter.

concept.whyItMatters: Holding database row locks across network calls or human think-time (like editing a document or checking out a shopping cart) stalls concurrent users and can saturate connection pools in milliseconds. Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC) eliminates lock waiting on the read path, achieving high throughput with a single round-trip compare-and-swap at write time.
whenToUse: Low-to-moderate contention workloads (conflict rate < 5–10%) such as user profile updates, CMS edits, or Kubernetes controller reconciliations.
Stateless HTTP/REST APIs where holding a database transaction open while a user edits a form is impossible—use `ETag` + `If-Match` headers.
Distributed NoSQL stores (DynamoDB, Cosmos DB, Cassandra) where cross-node pessimistic locks are expensive or unavailable.
whenNotToUse: High-contention hot keys (e.g., 500 concurrent requests decrementing a single flash-sale SKU or incrementing a global sequence) where >20% conflicts trigger retry storms.
Multi-record financial transfers requiring strict isolation across several rows where pessimistic locking or serializable transactions are simpler to reason about.
Operations with irreversible external side effects (charging a credit card, sending an email) inside the optimistic retry loop.
keyPoints: Every mutable record carries a monotonically increasing `version` integer, timestamp, or opaque `ETag` that changes on every successful write.
Reads are completely lock-free; the writer computes the new state in memory and issues a conditional write (`WHERE id = $1 AND version = $2`).
If 0 rows are affected (SQL) or `ConditionalCheckFailedException` (DynamoDB) / `412 Precondition Failed` (HTTP) is returned, the write is rejected.
Safe automatic retries require idempotent, side-effect-free computation and exponential backoff with full jitter to avoid synchronized retry thundering herds.
Never use client-supplied wall-clock timestamps (`updated_at`) for OCC comparisons—clock skew and 1ms collisions silently cause lost updates.

examples.title: Kubernetes Controller Reconciliation with `resourceVersion`
examples.scenario: Multiple controllers and `kubectl` users concurrently patch `Deployment` objects in the Kubernetes API server backed by etcd.
examples.outcome: etcd stores a monotonic `mod_revision` exposed as `metadata.resourceVersion`. Concurrent `PUT`/`PATCH` requests with a stale `resourceVersion` fail immediately with HTTP `409 Conflict`, forcing the controller to re-fetch the latest state and recompute its diff without holding locks.

examples.title: Preventing Lost Updates in a DynamoDB Wallet Service
examples.scenario: Two webhook handlers attempted to credit a merchant's balance simultaneously using a naive read-modify-write `PutItem`, overwriting each other's deposits.
examples.outcome: Adding `ConditionExpression: "version = :expected_v"` alongside `SET version = version + 1` eliminated lost updates in 1 RTT; conflicts stayed at 0.4% and resolved cleanly within 1–2 jittered retries.

tradeOffs.pro: Zero lock contention and 1-RTT writes when conflicts are rare.
tradeOffs.con: Under heavy contention (>20% conflict rate), wasted work and retries degrade throughput worse than queuing behind a pessimistic lock.

tradeOffs.pro: Works seamlessly across disconnected HTTP requests using `ETag` and `If-Match`.
tradeOffs.con: Users who spend 10 minutes editing a form get a `412 Precondition Failed` and must manually merge or reload.

tradeOffs.pro: Avoids deadlocks and lock-wait timeouts completely.
tradeOffs.con: Requires explicit retry loops (for automated workers) or conflict-resolution UI (for humans) on every write path.

failureModes.name: Retry Storm (Thundering Herd)
failureModes.description: 100 workers hit a conflict on the same record and immediately retry in a tight `while True` loop, multiplying DB load by 10x.
failureModes.mitigation: Cap retries (e.g., max 3–5 attempts) and apply exponential backoff with full jitter (`sleep(random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)))`).

failureModes.name: ABA / Timestamp Collision Problem
failureModes.description: Using `updated_at` timestamps instead of an integer `version` lets two writes within the same millisecond or across NTP clock drift pass the condition check.
failureModes.mitigation: Always use a strictly monotonic integer (`version = version + 1`) or storage-assigned revision/ETag.

failureModes.name: Side-Effect Duplication on Retry
failureModes.description: A worker charges a payment gateway, fails the DB version check, retries the whole function, and charges the customer twice.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep external side effects outside the OCC retry loop (e.g., use the Transactional Outbox pattern) or pass idempotency keys.

failureModes.name: Missing `If-Match` Enforcement in APIs
failureModes.description: Making `If-Match` optional allows old mobile clients to omit the header and silently overwrite newer server state.
failureModes.mitigation: Return `428 Precondition Required` when `If-Match` is missing on mutable `PUT`/`PATCH` endpoints.

commonMistakes: Incrementing `version` in application memory before checking it, or forgetting to include `AND version = :old_version` in the SQL `WHERE` clause.
Checking the affected row count incorrectly—many ORMs silently succeed on `UPDATE` affecting 0 rows unless you explicitly assert `rowsAffected == 1` (e.g., JPA `OptimisticLockingFailureException`).
Using OCC on a global counter or flash-sale inventory row where 1,000+ users contend on a single key.
Retrying indefinitely without a circuit breaker or max-attempt limit.
Returning `500 Internal Server Error` instead of `409 Conflict` or `412 Precondition Failed` when a version mismatch occurs.

sections.content:
## The idea

Formalized by Kung and Robinson (1981), **Optimistic Concurrency Control (OCC)** bets that conflicts between concurrent transactions are the exception rather than the rule.

Instead of acquiring locks before reading data, a transaction proceeds in three phases:
1. **Read**: Fetch the record and its current `version` (or `ETag`) without locking.
2. **Modify**: Compute the new state locally in memory.
3. **Validate & Commit**: Atomically write the new state *only if* the stored `version` still equals the version read in step 1, incrementing it to `version + 1` in the same atomic statement.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider two fulfillment workers (`Worker A` and `Worker B`) updating an order's shipping address and status simultaneously:

1. Both workers read `order_id = 9001` at `version = 42`.
2. `Worker A` executes `UPDATE orders SET status = 'PACKED', version = 43 WHERE id = 9001 AND version = 42`. Postgres acquires a brief row-level write lock, sees `version = 42`, updates the row, and returns `rows_affected = 1`.
3. 5ms later, `Worker B` executes `UPDATE orders SET address = 'BLR-2', version = 43 WHERE id = 9001 AND version = 42`. Postgres evaluates the `WHERE` predicate against the newly committed row (`version = 43`), finds 0 matching rows, and returns `rows_affected = 0`.
4. `Worker B` detects `rows_affected == 0`, sleeps for a jittered 18ms backoff, re-reads `order_id = 9001` at `version = 43`, applies its address change, and succeeds at `version = 44`.

edges.description: Worker A reads row 9001 and observes version=42 without acquiring any lock.

edges.label: 2. Read (v=42)

edges.description: Worker B also reads row 9001 at version=42 while Worker A is computing.

edges.label: 3. CAS v=42 -> 43 (OK)
edges.title: Worker A wins commit
edges.description: UPDATE ... WHERE version=42 affects 1 row and advances version to 43.

edges.label: 4. CAS v=42 -> 43 (0 rows)

edges.description: WHERE version=42 matches 0 rows because stored version is now 43.

edges.label: 5. Conflict -> Jittered Retry
edges.title: Re-read v=43 and commit v=44
edges.description: Worker B backs off with full jitter, re-reads v=43, and commits cleanly to v=44.

data.caption: Both workers read version 42 without locking; Worker A's atomic compare-and-swap advances the row to 43, forcing Worker B to re-read and retry.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / OCC across HTTP, SQL, and NoSQL
sections.content:
## OCC across HTTP, SQL, and NoSQL

The exact same compare-and-swap primitive appears under different names across protocols:

- **HTTP / REST (RFC 9110)**: Server returns `ETag: "v42"` on `GET`. Client sends `If-Match: "v42"` on `PUT`/`PATCH`; server returns `412 Precondition Failed` on mismatch.
- **PostgreSQL / MySQL**: `UPDATE items SET qty = $1, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $2 AND version = $3`. JPA automates this with `@Version`.
- **DynamoDB**: `ConditionExpression: "version = :v"` returning `ConditionalCheckFailedException`.
- **Redis**: `WATCH key` -> `MULTI` -> `SET key val` -> `EXEC` (returns `nil` if `key` changed between `WATCH` and `EXEC`).

## OCC vs. Pessimistic Locking

| Metric / Scenario | Optimistic (OCC) | Pessimistic (`FOR UPDATE`) |
|---|---|---|
| **Conflict Rate < 5%** | Optimal (1 RTT, no lock wait) | Extra lock-acquisition overhead |
| **Conflict Rate > 20%** | Severe CPU/DB waste from retries | Predictable queuing; higher effective throughput |
| **Deadlock Risk** | Zero (no lock hold-and-wait) | Possible on multi-row updates |
| **Human Think-Time (UI)** | Supported via `ETag` + `If-Match` | Dangerous (holds DB connections open) |
| **Failure Signal** | `0 rows affected` / `409` / `412` | Lock wait timeout / deadlock rollback |

## Failure modes

1. **Hot-Key Contention Collapse**: At 30%+ conflict rates, OCC spends more DB IOPS failing and re-reading than committing. Switch hot keys to pessimistic `FOR UPDATE`, atomic SQL increments (`SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE qty >= 1`), or a single-writer queue.
2. **Lost Updates via Nullable Versions**: Backfilling a `version` column with `NULL` breaks `WHERE version = NULL` in SQL (`NULL = NULL` evaluates to `UNKNOWN`). Always initialize `version BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1`.
3. **Retry Loops Without Jitter**: Fixed 50ms retries synchronize colliding workers into repeated collisions.

## Implementing jittered retries in Java/Python

Wrap only the pure read-compute-CAS block in a bounded retry helper (e.g., 3–5 attempts) using **full jitter**:

```python
for attempt in range(max_attempts):
    record = repo.get(order_id)
    updated = record.apply_change(cmd)
    if repo.compare_and_swap(updated, expected_version=record.version):
        return updated
    sleep_ms = random.uniform(0, min(cap_ms, base_ms * (2 ** attempt)))
    time.sleep(sleep_ms / 1000.0)
raise ConflictError("Max OCC retries exceeded")
```

Notice that external calls (HTTP webhooks, emails) must happen *after* `compare_and_swap` returns `True` (or be persisted in an outbox table within the same transaction).

## Practical checklist

- **Use monotonic integers (`BIGINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1`)** or server-generated ETags—never wall-clock timestamps.
- **Assert `rows_affected == 1`** on every SQL CAS update; treat `0` as a conflict exception.
- **Enforce `If-Match`** on public `PUT`/`PATCH` APIs and return `412 Precondition Failed` on mismatch.
- **Measure conflict rates**: Alert if OCC retry rates exceed 10% on any table so you can switch hot keys to pessimistic or atomic-delta patterns.
- **Keep side effects out of the retry loop** to prevent duplicate charges or notifications.

interviewProblems.title: Optimistic Concurrency Control
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Optimistic Concurrency Control. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A lock-free concurrency pattern that lets readers and writers proceed without blocking, validating at commit time via a version number or ETag that no one else modified the record.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Versioned Store applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Backoff & Jitter.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Backoff & Jitter experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Cap retries (e.g., max 3–5 attempts) and apply exponential backoff with full jitter (`sleep(random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)))`).

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Use atomic compare-and-swap (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` or HTTP `If-Match`) when conflicts are rare (<5%), and pair retries with exponential backoff and full jitter.
Avoid trap: Incrementing `version` in application memory before checking it, or forgetting to include `AND version = :old_version` in the SQL `WHERE` clause.

Avoid trap: Checking the affected row count incorrectly—many ORMs silently succeed on `UPDATE` affecting 0 rows unless you explicitly assert `rowsAffected == 1` (e.g., JPA `OptimisticLockingFailureException`).
When to reach for it: Low-to-moderate contention workloads (conflict rate < 5–10%) such as user profile updates, CMS edits, or Kubernetes controller reconciliations.
When to reach for it: Stateless HTTP/REST APIs where holding a database transaction open while a user edits a form is impossible—use `ETag` + `If-Match` headers.

putItTogether.title: Putting Optimistic Concurrency Control Together
putItTogether.summary: Use atomic compare-and-swap (`UPDATE ... WHERE id = ? AND version = ?` or HTTP `If-Match`) when conflicts are rare (<5%), and pair retries with exponential backoff and full jitter.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Optimistic Concurrency Control before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: etcd stores a monotonic `mod_revision` exposed as `metadata.resourceVersion`. Concurrent `PUT`/`PATCH` requests with a stale `resourceVersion` fail immediately with HTTP `409 Conflict`, forcing the controller to re-fetch the latest state and recompute its diff without holding locks.
